While I have logged hundreds of hours on this game, I cannot say I recommend it. If you've already purchased Cities Skylines 1 and have its DLCs, don't waste your money on this one.

The PR team is great at making platitudes of upcoming features and possible bug fixes. However, their latest QA post has essentially told the community that they are not committed to make the changes players really want to see. 

It seems the team is committed to releasing new DLCs instead of fixing issues in the base game, like, I don't know, the solar power plant or the mail system?

I had high hopes for this game, but the lack of support has left me disappointed.

- It regularly corrupts save files
- The simulation speed can slow down regardless of your computer’s specs, population size, or the number of elements
- It consumes a huge amount of resources
- There’s only one real DLC, and even that doesn’t add much to the experience
- The economy isn’t real

Pros:
+ the road-building tools are excellent

+ surfaces are customizable, and terrain can be painted
+ larger maps than in C:S I

I cannot recommend Cities: Skylines II based on the direction Paradox and Iceflake are communicating.

The biggest problem is not that the game receives no updates. It does. The problem is that, after months of Iceflake being in charge, the announced direction still looks far too unambitious for a game that needs fundamental improvement.

Many players come to Cities: Skylines to build beautiful, realistic, believable cities. Yet some of the systems that most directly limit that experience remain largely untouched.

Zoning is one of the clearest examples. The rigid zoning grid affects building placement, curved roads, block shapes, realistic suburbs, European-style streets, gaps between buildings, irregular parcels and the overall visual quality of a city. A serious zoning and parcel-generation overhaul could transform the game.

Instead, the official answer is essentially that smaller grids are not planned and better grid control is not even a short-term priority.

The same pattern appears elsewhere.

Major improvements to integrated public transport infrastructure? No big plans.

Tunnel and underground infrastructure improvements? Not currently.

Regional hierarchies with towns, villages and multiple settlements? No.

Major pathfinding rework? No.

Natural-disaster and evacuation improvements? Not planned.

More flexible road-building tools in normal gameplay? Maybe someday, while live editing is apparently out of scope.

Construction animations and more convincing citizen activity? Nothing scheduled.

What is actually being discussed is mostly incremental balancing, bug fixing, performance work, audio, lighting, textures, asset packs and smaller simulation adjustments.

Those things are welcome, but they are polish. They do not address many of the fundamental limitations that stop Cities: Skylines II from becoming the city builder it could have been.

What makes this even more frustrating is that the modding community has already demonstrated demand for much deeper control over roads, zoning, traffic, detailing, surfaces and placement. Mods are doing transformative work while the official roadmap appears focused on improving the existing framework rather than meaningfully expanding what players can build.

There is also a communication problem.

The official Steam Q&A directs players to continue discussion on the Paradox Forums, which requires a separate Paradox account, while discussion under the Steam announcement itself is locked.

For a company asking players to trust the long-term development of a troubled game, restricting discussion on the platform where many customers actually bought the game is a terrible approach. If you publish a Q&A on Steam, players should be able to discuss the answers on Steam.

I do not expect every community request to be implemented. I also understand that rewriting core systems is expensive and technically difficult.

But after this much time, I expected to see a much more ambitious vision for transforming the game: better zoning and parcel generation, greater road-building freedom, better terrain and building interaction, deeper traffic-management tools, more realistic city layouts and systems that genuinely expand the possibilities of city building.

Instead, the message currently feels like:

fix bugs, improve performance, polish visuals and audio, rely heavily on mods for advanced functionality, and keep releasing content around the same fundamental systems.

Maybe the upcoming roadmap will prove this assessment wrong. I hope it does.

But based on what Paradox and Iceflake are communicating today, I would strongly recommend that potential buyers look carefully at the current state of the game and the developers' stated plans before spending money on Cities: Skylines II or its additional content.

Do not buy it based on what you hope the game might become. Judge it based on what exists now and what the developers are actually committing to change.

Finally got this after having it on my wishlist for years. I’ve put just under 600 hours into CSL over 10 years, and have finally gotten all the DLC and modded it into the thermosphere. I waited on this due to its frankly abysmal launch and slow climb up to a more complete state, which has evidently greatly improved with Iceflake taking over development.

Performance and glitches are still a major issue. Unfortunately, this is still an issue even with the original as the level of agent-based simulation requires a beefy processor and lots of RAM. That said, the level of depth is far and above what the original vanilla game has: Industries and specializations are more complex, mixed-use zoning is fleshed out, and physical simulations like wind and water give much more consideration to how you lay out industrial areas, infrastructure, and emergency response systems.

Two relatively small changes make a big difference for me: deeper tax control and service import/exports. Being able to set taxes based on industry sector allows for much greater economic control, while eliminating density-based taxes for houses and businesses allows for more realistic cities that aren’t just skyscraper farms. Being able to import and export water and electricity also greatly improves regionalism and makes your city feel less like it exists in a vacuum.

On the note of QoL, transportation design is much better flushed out, and I greatly appreciate roundabouts being an upgrade to existing intersections rather than monstrous donuts clearing out whole neighborhoods. I also like the revision to district drawing, which functions more like polygon creation in a design program that gives much more precision compared to the blobby painting tools in the first game. I also really like the upgrade system and ability to assign service coverage on a district basis. Service control generally feels much more impactful as opposed to just slapping schools everywhere and calling it a day.

Perfect? Not at all, and there are things from the first game I sorely miss, such as those in the Airports and Campus DLC. The performance problems and lack of optimization are enormous elephants in the room but have been such keystone issues since launch that Iceflake will hopefully continue to improve upon. Also a small nit, but I’m just not a big fan of the radio stations this time around. CSL1’s were a mixed bag to be sure, but this time around they all seem to blend together in terms of genre, and are either so bland as to be forgettable or so grating that I end up switching them off and using modded stations instead. The DJ’s are at least far more tolerable to listen to.

I’d say a solid 7.25/10 for the time being. I’m a big enough fan to hang around for improvements, but I won’t count on anything earth-shattering in the near term.

Cities: Skylines II is part of a city-building series that most people probably already know thanks to Paradox. I never played the first game, and I only bought Cities: Skylines II after hearing that it had improved a lot compared to how it was at launch.

As someone jumping straight into the second game without any experience with the first one, I was honestly overwhelmed by the amount of information at the beginning. Still, I kept playing, experimenting, and learning how everything worked.

And honestly, I ended up really enjoying it.

Building a city can be extremely relaxing, but once traffic problems start appearing, the game suddenly turns into another learning experience. I had to figure out road layouts, intersections, public transportation, and how to plan everything more efficiently. Over time, I actually became addicted to that feeling of learning something new, applying it to my city, and then seeing the results.

Later on, I also installed quite a few mods, which made the overall experience much better.

That being said, the game's optimization is still pretty bad. I have a fairly powerful PC that can run most modern games at max settings without much trouble, but Cities: Skylines II still suffers from frequent FPS drops. It gets much worse as your city becomes larger and more populated. Running the game at 3x speed with a big city can honestly become a nightmare.

The AI also still has a lot of problems. Once the population grows and you start adding more services, traffic, public transport, and other things to manage, the game starts having more and more issues. Sometimes citizens, vehicles, or services just don't behave the way you expect them to, and it can become extremely frustrating.

At some point, it feels like the only way to keep your city working properly is to install mods to fix problems that really shouldn't need mods in the first place.

Overall, Cities: Skylines II is still a game I would recommend based on my experience. I had a lot of fun learning how to build and manage my city, and watching everything slowly grow was incredibly satisfying.

However, once my city reached around 200,000 population or more, the poor AI and performance issues started killing a lot of that enjoyment. Eventually, I decided to take a break because I didn't really want to install dozens of mods just to keep fixing problems with the game.

I really hope the developers continue improving the optimization and AI, because underneath all of these problems, Cities: Skylines II is genuinely a very enjoyable city-building game.

I really wanted to give this game a second chance, but there's still critical problems with the pathfinding/traffic AI that were there from the beginning that are still there. Restricted road/path types just do not actually work. Cars will drive on pedestrian-only roads, even when there is another option for them to get to their destinations. Pedestrians will cross roads when the crosswalks have been removed, even though I've built path bridges over the roads to all possible destinations (workaround I found is that roads with medians will actually work in stopping pedestrians from crossing without crosswalks, but that still limits the road types I can actually use).

There's also the visual glitches, two main ones:
- Many moving objects (cars, pedestrians) will leave behind a trail of afterimages. These afterimages disappear if the camera is moved.
- The wheels of vehicles become warped and jagged, twisting the geometry of the vehicles with them as they spin.

Cities: Skylines 2 — THE NEWEST AND BEST CITY BUILDER EVER!!
…sikeeeee. I wish.

I really wanted to love this game. I mean, the idea is there. Build a massive city, manage everything, watch your little civilization grow, and eventually create the city of your dreams.

Instead, I spend about 30 minutes playing and then find myself staring at the screen wondering what I'm supposed to be excited about.

And let's talk about the graphics.

MAXIMUM SETTINGS.
Everything is cranked to MAX.

And for what?

The graphics honestly look terrible for a game that demands this much performance.

I'm sitting here looking at my city thinking:

"Surely this can't be max settings..."

Meanwhile my RTX 5080 is sitting there wondering why it was summoned for a game that looks like it belongs on a very angry mobile phone.

RTX 5080: “I was built for this?”

Cities: Skylines 2:
“Yes. Now give me your entire GPU.”

This game somehow manages to make a high-end PC feel like it's running a mobile phone game. The graphics are honestly atrocious for what this game demands from your hardware. You'd think I'd be rendering the next Avatar movie with the amount of performance this thing wants.

But nope.

I'm building a city that looks like it was made in a microwave.

The performance is probably the biggest issue for me. A city builder should let you build a huge, beautiful city and then sit back and admire your creation. Instead, I'm watching my FPS slowly disappear as my population increases.

And somehow the game can be demanding AND boring at the same time.
That's an impressive achievement.

I usually get bored after around 30 minutes because there just isn't enough here to keep me invested for long sessions. The game has potential, but it feels like I'm playing a really expensive early-access tech demo that still has a LOT of work left to do.

There are plenty of things I like about the concept, and I can absolutely see the foundation of a great city builder underneath all of this.

But right now?

It needs A LOT more work.

Performance needs improvement. Graphics need improvement. Optimization needs improvement. And, honestly, the overall experience needs more things to make me actually want to keep playing.

I'll probably come back to it eventually.

Maybe after a few few few few more more more more updates.

Maybe after my grandchildren finish college.

2 years later I've come back again to see if they've fixed most (if not all) of the issues with it, and to see if it was up to the standard of Cities 1 and to be honest, I don't know what they've done for the last 2 years other than maybe add new assets to the game, the core game is still a broken mess

- There are still no premade roundabouts, so unless you want to make a boring grid city, you have to spend most of your time perfectly tweaking everything to make it sit properly

- Everything still violently snaps to the terrain, including underground placement, bridge heights and anything that has any interaction with the camera, meaning that if your city has any terrain deviation, especially if it's cliffs/large drops, you'll find yourself wanting to throw up all the time, if you can even navigate it at all

- Bridge heights themselves are capped at a certain level unless you add a massive pillar of dirt, then suddenly the sky is the limit, or rather, the dirt pillar

- The UI is still bright, garish and incredibly hard to parse at a glance, especially when trying to zone, everything is just bright green and short of looking at the building architecture style, it's near impossible to tell what's already zoned where

- Objects still "overlapp" other random objects that have no correlation to the object you're trying to place - You try to move a building and it tells you it's not possible because it overlapps a piece of road a kilometre away, for some reason

- Pedestrians completely ignore road markings and just do what they want (I had this issue with cars the first time around and while I didn't specifically test it this time, I have no reason to think that would be fixed this time if the pedestrians had the same issue)

- More of a personal thing, but having metro stations require subway yards now is incredibly annoying when trying to design a nice clean, concise city, especially since you can't put the subway yards underground (to my knowledge)

- The performance still leaves a lot to be desired - I have a fairly middle of the range PC that should handle it just fine but it constantly hangs and freezes, even on the lowest settings

- Why oh why did they remove the zoning brush? - Genuinely, what possible benefit is there to having to only use the marquee tool, the fill bucket or the single square brush?
One of the best things about Cities: Skylines was always the fact that you could build cities that weren't just grid cities, you could make free flowing, natural cities with curves, but now you're punished for doing that because you have to awkwardly go around with the fill bucket, filling out the zoning whenever you do a new area, it makes no sense that it was removed in the sequel

I know this is a big, possibly ranty review, and a number of these things might not bother you at all, but it's just so disappointing from the people who brought us one of the greatest city builders in the history of gaming, to follow up with this, and that's the crux of the problem.
It's not that any of these things are necessarily the end of the world or that they make it completely unplayable, but they're mostly large, structural issues with the game that weren't an issue in the first game, haven't been addressed at all, and make the whole thing just a worse experience than the first game, some of which feel like they would be the quickest and easiest solves to implement.

Too many bugs in the game, still after all this time it has been out. Yes, I have played many, many hours of it, but most of those hours come from simply letting the simulation run while I sleep or go to work. The biggest issue that I have is how stupid the citizens are. I give them free parking and put roads with parking as well as parking lots near medium and high density buildings. Citizens will instead park 10KM or more away and then "death march" home or to work. 
Recently I ran into a traffic jam and zoomed in to find some elderly woman walking down the middle of the road on her way to the elementary school for some reason. Yeah, because that's what some old woman needs to be doing. I wish the police would have just arrested her. Instead I had to watch her slowly walk while none of the traffic would go around her at all. 
The numbers are usually lies. Such as the amount of births, deaths, people moving in and moving away. The numbers will show things that say my population is growing, yet my population slowly decreases. I watched one simulation go from 10k people to nothing at a loss of 4/h. There was no reason for this, as the numbers clearly showed I should have been gaining about 200-300/h, instead it was a slow trickle that resulted in a ghost town. This simulation has potential, but I think the developers simply gave up. It's pretty clear that they don't play their game at all. I'm guessing they learned by following EA.

EDIT: It gets WORSE, believe it or not. Whenever a car accident happens, which they seem to happen more frequently than one would think, the game assigns a road maintenance vehicle to attend to the crash site. That's nice, but the vehicle never changes their assignment to take care of the accident. Instead, the road maintenance vehicle just continues doing its normal job while the accident backs traffic up until the game despawns the vehicles involved. 
If you decide that you want to handle traffic issues by using buses, watch out! On a normal, 2-lane road a bus stop will add a small section for the bus to pull off to the side to pick up people waiting at the stop. Well, the fun part is that cars will use this additional lane and back up the buses that want to pick up people waiting. They will go down the road, then switch to the new "bus lane", just to then get stuck trying to merge back over. I mean, I've seen this type of behavior from people, but seriously guys, this is stupid to see in a game. I still stand by what I said earlier, these developers do not play their game at all. I really hope the city building games coming out provide good competition. This game is garbage.
